D1: identical scripted scenarios and the same 20 planted errors were processed by both vendors with consistent simulated roles (Methods), so case-mix and specialty confounding are controlled by design; residual issue is the small investigator-built error set; D2: the 5 scenarios and 20 errors (9 omissions, 7 substitutions, 4 additions) were developed by the investigators modelled on prior studies (Methods) - a selected, not sampled, error set; D3: exposure is the vendor pipeline applied to the recorded encounters; vendors anonymised, Vendor B identified only as GPT-4o-based and model versions are those active in August 2025 (Methods; Discussion); adjudicated low; D4: no co-interventions - the same recordings were played to both systems and final notes (not intermediate transcripts) were evaluated (Methods; Discussion); D5: all 20 errors x 2 vendors were coded; interrater agreement 97.5% (39/40) with the single discrepancy resolved by consensus (Results); D6: sampling - census of all planted errors in 5 scripted scenarios, no sampling of real notes; reference standard - the original scripted statements and the interpreted exchange (ground truth by construction); grader blinding - 2 investigators independently reviewed all notes but blinding to vendor is not stated and the investigators built the scripts, and borderline unsupported-denial cases turn on a judgement call (Table 1 footnote) - mitigated by dual independent coding, consensus and a full sensitivity analysis recoding those cases; adjudicated moderate; D7: no registration or analysis plan; results reported by error type and by speaker context plus the sensitivity analysis, with no sign of selective omission

D1: consultation duration compared on aggregated data with 'no adjustment at the clinician or visit level' and authors state differences 'may be influenced by unmeasured factors such as clinician-specific practices, specialty, or visit type' (Discussion, Limitations); baseline documentation load and specialty mix (protocol confounders) uncontrolled; D2: 'use was not mandated and depended on clinician preference' (Methods 2.1) and selective use at the individual encounter level 'cannot be excluded' (Discussion), so Scribe consultations are self-selected and likely differ systematically; adjudicated serious; D3: modality taken from aggregated operational activity data (Methods 2.2, 2.4); partial or mixed use within a consultation is not described; D4: the system 'underwent iterative updates to its ASR and LLM components' during the 16 months (Methods 2.3) and minor EHR template adaptations were made before deployment (Discussion) - intervention not stable over the period; D5: analysis used 'complete aggregated corporate data' (Methods 2.1) but missingness in the operational datasets is not described; adjudicated moderate; D6: duration is an operational log measure taken the same way for both modalities, but only weighted monthly means are reported with no variance; D7: no registration or plan; overall weighted means and the month-by-month pattern (7 months faster with Scribe) are both reported (Results 3.3)

D1: agreement is measured within Scribe notes only (no comparator), so confounding acts through case and specialty mix - specialty agreement ranged 84.7% (Internal Medicine) to 92.6% (Otolaryngology) (Results 3.4); D2: fields analysed are those from self-selected Scribe consultations (Methods 2.1-2.2), which may be easier encounters; D3: Scribe use classified from operational data as for time; the metric is computed by Scribe's internal validation workflow (Methods 2.5); D4: iterative ASR/LLM updates during the period (Methods 2.3) could shift agreement over time; monthly values stayed within 87.4-89.2%; D5: field-level missingness and exclusions from the similarity calculation are not described; D6: sampling - all Scribe fields in the aggregated dataset, no independent sample; reference standard - 'the clinician-validated field represents the final version after review and editing of the AI-generated draft', i.e. the tool's own draft edited, not an independent ground truth, and embeddings come from the same NLP pipeline, which the authors state 'may lead to an overestimation of agreement' (Discussion, Limitations); grader blinding - no human grader, automated cosine similarity, so no blinding issue but no independent adjudication either; D7: no registration or plan; monthly series, global average (89.32%) and specialty range all reported

D1: two independent cross-sections, not paired measurements, with different eligibility (Round 1 more than 20 consultations, Round 2 more than 50) and no pre-deployment baseline - authors state differences 'may partly reflect differences in respondent composition rather than within-individual changes' (Discussion, Limitations); maturation over time is inseparable from composition change; D2: voluntary surveys with response rates 14.7% (184/1255) in Round 1 and 7.8% (163/2093) in Round 2 - authors note possible 'overrepresentation of more engaged users or those with more favorable perceptions' (Discussion); D3: exposure strata defined by cumulative Scribe consultations (advanced more than 300, medium 150-300, basic more than 50) from operational data (Methods 2.6); the Round 1 vs Round 2 contrast itself is a time contrast, not a use contrast; D4: system updates between rounds (Methods 2.3) are part of the maturation the authors invoke; no documentation training or staffing co-interventions reported; D5: item-level missing data are not reported and non-response (85-92%) is unaddressed analytically; adjudicated serious; D6: self-reported 0-10 experience domains from unblinded users (the outcome is perception itself); instrument reliability was excellent (Cronbach alpha 0.937 and 0.935) and the domain profile was stable across rounds (r=0.962) (Results 3.5); D7: no registration or plan; all 7 domains plus the composite are reported with Welch P values, Hedges g and FDR q values, including the 2 non-significant domains (Table 1)

D1: no comparator notes (no manual/human-note arm); quality is post-only self-audit, so period and case-mix confounding cannot be separated; D2: adjudicated serious: volunteer pilot providers; note sample is drawn only from participating providers' AI notes; D3: notes are Abridge-generated notes in the pilot; product and period clear (Methods); D4: onboarding/training accompanied use; no other pre-set co-interventions reported; D5: adjudicated moderate: 494 notes analysed (Results/Table 2) but the sampling frame and the share of the >25600 pilot notes this represents, and any missing audits, are not fully described; Discussion calls them 'random notes' without a sampling method in Methods; D6 (note-audit addition): sampling - provider self-auditing of notes, described as random in Discussion only; reference standard - the provider's own review of the note before submission, with no encounter audio/record reference standard stated; grader blinding - none, providers graded their own notes knowing the tool, unblinded; authors: 'self-auditing notes for safety are similarly prone to bias. This form of note evaluation is suboptimal' (Limitations); D7: no registration/plan stated; accuracy, thoroughness, tone and edit-extent results all reported in Table 2

Outcome group is patient experience (the study's only protocol outcome), assessed here under quality per the batch group list. D1: adjudicated moderate: difference-in-differences with controls matched on specialty, >=30 surveys and similar pre-pilot ratings, parallel trends checked graphically ('monthly percentages... stable with no discernable trends', Methods) and patient characteristics similar (Table S1); residual concern is volunteer pilot physicians, acknowledged: 'physicians volunteered to participate in the pilot, they and their patients could have differed from controls' (Discussion); D2: pilot physicians volunteered; surveys unavailable for 3 pilot physicians; patient survey responders are older, White, female and from less disadvantaged areas (Results/Discussion), a measurement-sample selection issue shared across groups; D3: scribe use tracked at every visit and pilot surveys included 'only when the encounter used the AI scribe' (Methods); controls are non-pilot physicians; D4: adjudicated low: visit-by-visit discretion and patient consent are the pilot intervention as designed; no pre-set co-interventions (documentation training, template or staffing changes) reported in either group; D5: routine voluntary patient surveys; response denominators vary by item and period (Table 1) and per-group response rates are not reported, so missingness could relate to satisfaction; D6: validated CAHPS-type items with conventional top-box scoring (Methods); patients consented to scribe use so were aware of it, which could influence ratings, but instrument and scoring are identical across groups and periods; D7: adjudicated moderate: no registration or published analysis plan stated (Pass B: low because all 5 prespecified items are reported in full in Tables 1-2, including null results)

D1: sequential non-randomised cohorts (unprompted Feb-Apr vs prompted Jun-Aug 2025) with period effects and case-mix differences printed in Table 2 (cases per board 32.75 vs 18.25; oral cavity 35.1% vs 17.8%; pathology reviewed 48.1% vs 50.7%, imaging 64.9% vs 87.7%); no adjustment; authors list 'period effects, selection bias, and learning contamination' (Limitations); D2: all eligible cases in each period deployed to the study (Methods); D4: adjudicated moderate: prompting is the intervention; the prompt template was developed from preliminary results and authors note prompting may itself have structured presentations (Discussion), a co-effect of the intervention as designed rather than an extraneous co-intervention; no training/template/staffing changes beyond prompting reported; D5: all discussed cases scored; rubric criteria scored NA when not mentioned at tumor board (Table 1 footnote), which explains varying criterion denominators; no missing-score problem stated; D6 (note-audit addition): sampling - consecutive eligible cases in each cohort period (131/73/48/81 patients); reference standard - the Zoom recording of the discussion ('Scoring occurred after tumor board using the zoom recording as reference', Methods); grader blinding - raters (A.M. and S.A.) trained on the rubric and 'blinded to whether cases were documented manually or with ambient AI and to whether tumor boards were discussed with or without prompting', but each case was reviewed by 1 rater and inter-rater reliability could not be assessed (Methods/Limitations); rubric is an adapted, unvalidated MODe-based tool with equal domain weights (Limitations) - adjudicated moderate; D7: no registration (QI study); primary/secondary outcomes prespecified in Methods and domain, criterion and total results reported with FDR-adjusted q values (Tables 3-4)

D1: sequential cohorts as for quality; discussion and administrative time are sensitive to case mix and board size, which differ across cohorts (Table 2: mean board length 96m 34s unprompted vs 62m 35s prompted; cases per board 32.75 vs 18.25); no adjustment; D2: adjudicated moderate: all eligible cases included per period; the paired administrative-time comparison uses the 2-board subset whose selection is not stated; D3: arms defined by documentation method and phase as for quality (Methods); D4: prompting phase change as for quality; no other pre-set co-interventions reported; D5: discussion and administrative time recorded per case for all cohorts (Table 2), no missing data reported; D6: adjudicated moderate: discussion time is recorded per case on the same basis, but administrative time is defined differently by arm - manual: 'time taken to manually write up the tumor board discussion while referencing the recordings'; AI: 'Abridge processing time and reviewer time required to validate the generated summary' (Methods) - so the paired contrast mixes writing time with processing-plus-review time (Pass B: serious on this point); D7: no registration (QI); time outcomes are prespecified secondary outcomes and are reported for all cohorts including null primary-cohort results (p=0.158, Table 2)

D1: adjudicated serious: uncontrolled pre-post with no concurrent control; pre/post periods differ by wave (2-7 months) across Feb 2024-Oct 2025; GEE adjusts LASSO-selected age, sex, practice setting, duration since ADT initiation and MTDM experience (Methods/Table 2), but baseline documentation load is handled only by the within-pharmacist pre period and period/secular effects remain; authors note oversampling of early adopters (Limitations); D2: Waves 1-3 purposive, Wave 4 'all Geisinger MTDM pharmacists with an iOS device who requested ADT' (Methods) - self-selection of keen users; analysis limited to 30/41 licence holders with usable survey + Signal data; D3: ADT activation and eligible encounters defined in Epic Signal; utilisation 64.8% (Table 2); product (Abridge) and licence activation dates clear; D4: adjudicated moderate: minimal out-of-the-box training and Haiku configuration described (Methods); no documentation training, template or staffing changes reported - SmartText/SmartPhrase use varied by pharmacist and is described qualitatively; Pass B recorded no information; D5: 11/41 pharmacists excluded because pre/post surveys could not be combined with Signal data (Results: 30 usable, 73% response); time outcome is system-recorded for the analysed 30, but reasons for exclusion beyond survey completion are not detailed; D6: Epic Signal objective timing, but authors and interviewees state Signal aggregates Note and Letter activities plus adjacent navigation and pauses after 5 seconds of inactivity, likely underestimating documentation time (Discussion, citing Epic logic); same system pre and post; D7: no registration/protocol stated; utilisation and time outcomes reported in full in Table 2 with adjusted and unadjusted tests

Workload (NASA-TLX Documentation Burden) is grouped under burnout per the batch instructions. D1: uncontrolled pre-post as for time; no adjustment for survey outcomes beyond paired tests; baseline burden, specialty mix and self-selection unaddressed (Methods, Data Analysis); D2: purposive plus self-requested (iOS, requested ADT) waves and analysis restricted to survey completers (30/41) as for time; D3: adjudicated low: exposure is ADT licence activation with Signal-measured utilisation per pharmacist (Table 2); Pass B concern was self-reported use in interviews, which does not classify the survey exposure; D4: minimal training as for time; no other pre-set co-interventions reported; D5: adjudicated moderate: paired pre/post surveys required, 73% usable response (30/41); non-completers excluded with no comparison of their baseline scores reported, so outcome-related missingness cannot be excluded but is not demonstrated; D6: Documentation Burden uses the validated NASA-TLX (summed effort, mental and temporal demand) and burnout the Mini-Z single item dichotomised at >3 (Methods/Table 3); both are unblinded self-report from volunteer users expecting benefit, and the paper lists self-report biases (recall, social desirability, priming) as threats (Limitations) - adjudicated serious for these perception outcomes; after-hours documentation in this study is also a pharmacist estimate (survey), not a Signal measure; D7: no registration/protocol stated; all five survey variables are reported in Table 3 including the null Patient Access and non-significant burnout results, with effect sizes and CIs

D1: Only one physician per language group; paper states language is confounded with individual characteristics (typing speed, familiarity, style) and actor-case assignments were not systematically recorded (Limitations); no adjustment for baseline documentation load. D2: Two department consultants completed all workflows; simulated cases balanced per consultant (6 each) but participant selection process not described (Methods, Participants). D3: Four workflows defined in detail with technology and physician role tabled (Table 1); Whisper Large v3 used out of the box with no fine-tuning in Workflows 3-4. D4: Controlled simulated setting, same prompts/parameters for all cases and no mid-study prompt editing; no co-interventions (training, templates, staffing) described. D5: All 12 encounters and 48 notes accounted for; no missing outcome data reported. D6: Independent observer timed documentation with a stopwatch and background processing was excluded by a pre-set definition (Efficiency Measurement), but the timekeeper and participants were not blinded and Hawthorne effects are acknowledged (Limitations) - Pass B rated this serious for unblinded timing; adjudicated moderate because the measure is a stopwatch with fixed definitions. D7: No registration or analysis plan stated; primary outcome and nonparametric model pre-described in Methods and post-hoc pairwise tests used Dunn with Bonferroni correction.

D1: Same confounding as the time outcome: one physician per language group, confounded with individual traits, actor-case assignments not recorded (Limitations). D2: Two consultants and 12 simulated cases balanced per consultant; selection process not described. D3: Workflows and note-generation pipeline defined (Table 1; LLM Pipeline); Workflow 2 notes are both a comparator and the reference standard for two PDQI items (see D6). D4: Same prompt stack and parameters for all cases; no co-interventions in the simulated setting. D5: All 48 notes scored by all three LLM raters; no missing scores reported. D6: Measurement is not valid for a quality claim: three LLM raters had Krippendorff alpha -0.433 (95% CI -0.444 to -0.416), i.e. systematic disagreement; for Accuracy and Thoroughness there was no ground-truth transcript and scores reflect perceived plausibility, and Workflow 2 automatically received 5/5 for Lack of Hallucination and Lack of Bias while Workflows 1, 3 and 4 were scored against it (Quality Assessment; Results). Pass A rated critical on the authors' own statement that the scores preclude definitive conclusions; Pass B rated serious; adjudicated critical. Note-audit addition: sampling - all 48 notes (12 per workflow); reference standard - corresponding Workflow 2 note for hallucination/bias only, no encounter ground truth for the other 8 items; grader blinding - LLM raters, no human grader, workflow identity inherent in the scoring instructions. D7: No registration or plan; quality labelled exploratory by the authors, but all 10 criteria and totals are reported.

D1: Single-group pre-post with no concurrent control in the available text; none of the pre-set confounders (baseline documentation load, specialty mix, concurrent EHR changes, self-selection) is addressed in the available text (Abstract, Program Description/Evaluation). D2: Efficiency analysis was on a subset of the 97 participating clinicians; how the subset was formed is not described in the available text, so self-selection cannot be excluded. D3: Two commercial tools (Vendor A, Vendor B) are distinguished and utilisation compared, but clinician-level crossover/mixed use is not described in the available text. D4: Training/onboarding and technical support were programme components; concurrent EHR, template or staffing changes are not reported in the available text - no information. D5: Missing data, clinician attrition and note denominators are not reported in the available text - Pass A: no information; Pass B: serious for an unreported subset analysis; adjudicated no information because the full text (Table 1) was not available to either pass. D6: Outcome is EHR-based documentation time per note and per day (objective audit-log type measure), but metric definitions are not given in the available text. D7: No registration stated; evaluation framed by OKR metrics, but Table 1 and the full outcome set are in the paywalled full text and could not be checked against a plan - Pass A: serious; Pass B: no information; adjudicated serious because selective reporting cannot be excluded from the available record. NOTE: all judgements are limited by the subscription-preview source; see batch4_studies.csv unparsed_or_thin_note.

D1: Analysis is restricted to self-selected active users with no non-user comparator; licences were voluntary and encouraged by leadership (Methods). Interrupted time series handles secular trend in form, but baseline documentation load, specialty mix and concurrent EHR changes are not adjusted for; pre-set confounder self-selection of keen users is built into the cohort. D2: Cohort required use for 25 or more encounters in at least 1 month - selection on post-adoption use, which is tied to the outcome; only about 8% of system clinicians were active users (Results). Pass B rated moderate (threshold pre-stated as an eligibility rule); adjudicated serious because the threshold is defined by post-baseline behaviour. D3: DAX Copilot use and first active use are defined from EHR metadata and licence activation from January 1 2024 (Methods). D4: Leadership encouragement is described; documentation training, template changes, staffing changes and other concurrent EHR changes in the period are not reported - moderate. D5: 16149 observations from 1547 clinicians are reported, but missing-data share and handling per outcome are not described - moderate. D6: Outcomes are EHR audit-log minutes (TIN per appointment, after-hours minutes) and defined productivity fields (CEP, APD, RVU) in Table 2; measurement does not depend on clinician self-report and is the same pre and post. D7: No registration; SQUIRE quality-improvement reporting stated and outcomes pre-listed in Methods with ITS details in Supplement 1, but there is no analysis plan to check the paired and ITS presentations against - moderate.

D1: DAX vs non-DAX encounters are concurrent, not randomised; models adjust for appointment length, appointment hour and provider clustering (random intercepts), but baseline documentation load, encounter complexity and case mix beyond length are unmeasured, and repeat users differ from non-adopters (Methods; Table 2). D2: Comparative analysis is restricted to 6 of 29 providers who used DAX more than twice - selection on post-implementation behaviour tied to perceived benefit and workflow fit (Results, Adoption Patterns). D3: DAX encounters identified through system metadata and categorised by appointment length (Methods) - classification is clean. D4: Institution-wide rollout included standardised training resources (videos, guides, webinars, helpdesks); DAX does not retain Epic dot phrases/SmartPhrases, so clinicians had to rebuild templates - a co-occurring workflow change described in the Discussion; staffing changes not reported - moderate. D5: Missing-data share and handling for encounter metadata are not described - moderate. D6: Documentation time is active editing time from system metadata (objective), and closure is a timestamp outcome; however the paper notes closure is intentionally delayed pending laboratory results, so closure measures workflow as well as scribe effect - moderate. D7: No registration or analysis plan stated; Results text unadjusted closure percentages (9.4% vs 34.2%; 47.8% vs 80.8%) conflict with Table 1 counts/percentages (7.7% vs 21.5%; 46.1% vs 60.5%) with no explanation - Pass A: moderate; Pass B: serious; adjudicated serious for unexplained inconsistent reporting of a reported outcome.

D1: Single-arm study with no measured comparator: the comparator is modelled manual typing, so baseline documentation load, clinician mix (trainees 74.6% of use vs consultants) and concurrent ED changes cannot be separated from the scribe effect (Methods; Results). D2: Use was completely voluntary and only 20 of 63 clinicians with access used the system (9/40 consultants, 11/23 trainees); hospital medical officers and interns did not take part (Methods; Limitations) - self-selection of keen users. D3: Scribe use is captured by the software for each presentation, but a capture could be ambient listening, dictation, or a mix of both (Methods) - moderate. D4: An educational session and vendor one-on-one training/troubleshooting occurred in the pilot week, whose data were excluded, and no vendor contact occurred during data collection (Methods) - co-intervention largely contained, moderate. D5: Final notes were manually extracted with 10% independently double-extracted with complete agreement; missing encounters/notes are not described - moderate. D6: The time outcome is not measured: it is modelled from assumed typing speeds (52/65 WPM), reading speed (238 WPM) and a 10 s generation time, with speeds taken from the general population, and the authors state this may over- or underestimate true performance (Methods; Limitations). Pass A: serious; Pass B: critical because no documentation time was observed at all; adjudicated serious because the model, inputs and arithmetic are fully transparent and the direction is consistent across both speed assumptions. D7: No registration or analysis plan stated; uptake, word counts, edit counts and both typing-speed scenarios are all reported - moderate.

D1: Scenario content is standardised within each analysis (same scenarios across personality types; verbatim transcripts across accents), which controls clinical content; however personality and accent analyses used partially overlapping scenario sets, accent strength was not formally validated and scenario effects were present (Methods; Limitations) - moderate. D2: Simulated consultations with trained actors and read human-accent speech are a selected, orderly sample that under-represents real practice (overlapping talk, interruptions, carers); scenario and accent sets were selected pragmatically (Methods; Limitations) - moderate. D3: A single CAIS in its default configuration with the SOAP template was used throughout; the integrated speech-recognition component is unspecified (Methods) - intervention as evaluated is defined, low. D4: Controlled laboratory: same room, hardware and standardised microphone placement across conditions; no co-interventions - low. D5: The number of recordings/summaries contributing to each analysis is stated (20 personality; 70 accents), but missing or failed outputs are not reported - Pass A: moderate; Pass B: no information; adjudicated moderate. D6: Note-audit addition - sampling: all CAIS summaries from the standardised consultations were marked (20 personality; 70 accent consultations); reference standard: human-verified ground-truth transcript for personality, but a scenario-specific reference summary deemed by the authors to contain the pertinent information for accents (not the full transcript), and ground-truth transcripts for impairment recognition; grader blinding: who counted the errors and whether they knew the personality/accent condition is not stated in the main text, and clinical severity of errors was not graded (authors state error counts reflect frequency, with clinical risk unquantified) - serious. D7: No registration or analysis plan stated; headline medians and p values are in the text but most per-condition results sit in figures and online supplemental tables S1-S7, so completeness of reporting cannot be verified from the article text - Pass A: moderate; Pass B: serious; adjudicated moderate.

D1: No comparator; error proportions within AI notes only, specialty/case mix unadjusted (family/internal medicine contributed 83.4% of evaluated notes, Table 3); D2: '31 physicians volunteered for the pilot program' - self-selected early adopters (Methods; Discussion limitation 1); D3: Scribe use defined for all pilot notes (7545 AI-generated notes, Results); D4: No co-interventions (training/template/staffing changes) reported in the 2-month pilot; D5: Only 356/7545 notes (4.7%) evaluated, most physicians assessed fewer than the requested 20 notes despite reminders; 9 assessments unlinkable (Methods/Discussion); D6 (note-audit addition): Sampling - physicians asked to evaluate 10 draft notes on 2 days in a 3-week period (convenience subset, 4.7%); Reference standard - physician's own recollection of their own visit, no transcript/audio reference; Grader blinding - none, physicians graded their own notes with an unvalidated novel instrument, severity by individual clinical judgement (Methods; Discussion limitation 3-4); D7: No registration or pre-set analysis plan; quality-improvement project with instrument developed for the pilot (Methods)

D1: No comparator; quality score summarised for AI notes only, no adjustment for specialty or baseline documentation load (Table 3); D2: '31 physicians volunteered' - self-selected early adopters, differential assessment response (Methods; Discussion); D3: Scribe use defined for all pilot notes; D4: No co-interventions reported; D5: Quality score available only for the 356 evaluated notes; vendor edited-% available for only 960/7545 notes (12.7%) due to technical issues (Results); D6: Quality score derived from the same unvalidated physician survey (score = sum of 1-(0.2 x severity) components, Methods); physicians graded their own notes unblinded; vendor edited-% is an indirect quality proxy calculated by the vendor; D7: No registration/analysis plan reported

D1: Benchmark contrasts are within-transcript (same 420 constructed scenarios across models/prompts), controlling encounter content; only 10 base encounters, so topic/relationship mix is fixed by construction (Section 2.1); D2: All 420 constructed test transcripts (10 patients x 6 relationships x 7 topics) entered every model condition; no participant selection (Section 2.1); D3: Models, versions and prompt conditions fully specified; temperature 0 (Sections 2.2.1-2.2.2); D4: No co-interventions; single-turn generation as specified; D5: Complete benchmark outputs; no missing data reported; D6 (note-audit addition): Sampling - all generated notes assessed automatically, no sampling; Reference standard - known injected third-party information (gold-standard by construction); Grader blinding - automated detector (semantic search tau=0.4 + spaCy specificity extraction), validated by human annotation of 100 positive and 100 negative samples (precision 86%, recall 84%, Section 2.3.1.1), so ~1 in 6 leaks may be missed; D7: No registration or pre-set analysis plan; multiple prompt conditions and exploratory analyses reported (Sections 2-3)

D1: Within-transcript paired comparisons across prompt conditions; encounter content fixed by benchmark construction (Section 2.1); D2: All 420 transcripts in every condition; no selection; D3: Models/prompts fully specified (Section 2.2); D4: No co-interventions in the primary single-turn settings; D5: No missing outputs reported; D6: Reference-based metrics only - ROUGE-1 plus GPT-4o-mini decompose-then-verify conciseness/completeness against the original aci-bench reference notes (Section 2.3.2); no human quality grading and no validation of the quality metrics against clinician judgement reported; D7: No registration/plan; quality reported alongside many leakage conditions and exploratory two-step/Other-section analyses, emphasis in text is selective (Sections 3.2, 3.5)

D1: Same 4 standardised RACGP cases used for every scribe, so case mix is held constant; no adjustment beyond repeated-measures design (Methods); D2: All 20 notes (4 cases x 5 scribes) rated by all 3 raters; no selection after generation (Methods); D3: Scribes defined (4 anonymised commercial AI products, most up-to-date paid versions, default settings; 1 human scribe), outputs presented 'as is' without edits (Methods); D4: No co-interventions; default settings by design; D5: Complete ratings for all notes/domains; ICCs reported (Table 4); D6: Modified PDQI-9 not formally re-validated after adding 2 domains; raters blinded to note source and viewed the consultation video before rating (strong reference), but inter-rater reliability only moderate overall (ICC 0.56-0.58) and poor for several domains (Methods; Table 4; Discussion); D7: No registration; primary/secondary outcomes pre-stated in the paper and all 10 domains reported (Table 3)

D1: Same 4 standardised cases for all scribes; case mix constant (Methods); D2: All 20 notes rated; no selection; D3: Scribe classification clean; products anonymised but consistent (Methods); D4: No co-interventions; D5: Complete ratings; D6 (note-audit addition): Sampling - all 20 generated notes audited, no sampling; Reference standard - video recording of the consultation viewed before rating, hallucination defined as content 'only contains information verifiable by the transcript'; Grader blinding - raters blinded to note source and product; BUT the freedom-from-hallucination domain is one of two newly added, unvalidated PDQI-9 domains with poor inter-rater reliability (ICC 0.30, Table 4), so error measurement itself is unreliable; D7: No registration; domain reported with all other domains (Table 3)

D1: Randomisation by research team using a randomization app (Randomizer) before the surgeon entered the room; no allocation concealment described; baseline characteristics comparable (P>0.05, Table 1) (Methods); D2: Surgeon and research team unblinded (unavoidable for a scribe); patients blinded; no deviations from intended documentation method reported; analysis includes all 279 randomised patients; D3: 12/291 enrolled patients excluded for missing data before randomisation counts (279 analysed of 291); Table 2 implies ~150 letters/group vs 139/140 randomised - outcome-data denominators unclear; D4: Timing recorded by the unblinded research team/senior author present at all consultations (primary outcome timing not blinded, Methods), though start/stop rules were pre-specified per group; D5: Trial registered (NCT07489469) but no published analysis plan cited; multiple time and quality outcomes reported with P values

D1: Randomisation via app before each consultation; baseline comparable (Table 1); D2: Unblinded delivery; the surgeon reviewed AI letters and edited mistakes immediately as part of the intervention workflow in both groups' usual process; no crossovers reported; D3: 12 excluded for missing data; error denominators per letter set unclear (see time row); D4 (note-audit addition): Sampling - every letter in both groups reviewed; Reference standard - surgeon's own knowledge of the encounter (no independent transcript reference); Grader blinding - medical errors assessed by the (unblinded) surgeon: paper states 'the evaluation of medical notes may have been subject to observer bias, as the reviewing surgeon was aware of which notes were generated by the AI scribe' (Limitations); spelling/grammar assessed by unblinded researchers, with allocation revealed to senior authors only after those evaluations (Methods, contradictory reporting); D5: Registered trial; medical-error outcome pre-stated among secondary objectives; error types not split (no omissions/hallucinations/inclusions breakdown)

D1: Randomisation via app; baseline comparable (Table 1); D2: Unblinded delivery inherent to the intervention; letters finalised through the usual review process in both arms; D3: 12 missing-data exclusions; quality denominators follow the letter set analysed in Tables 4-5; D4: Quality graded by ChatGPT on blinded letters ('their blinded consultation letters were going to be uploaded to ChatGPT'), an automated grader without knowledge of allocation, though the paper notes AI vs conventional letters are fairly easy to distinguish; human spelling/grammar grading was unblinded; D5: Registered trial; all six ChatGPT quality dimensions reported in full (Table 5)

D1: Pre-set confounders partly handled: clinician and month fixed effects, adjustment for weekly visit volume, parallel pretrends supported in event study; specialty/sex/use-intensity examined in interactions. BUT adoption was by clinician opt-in (self-selection of keen users) and the paper concedes unobserved confounders cannot be ruled out and baseline documentation load is not directly modelled (Methods; Limitations); D2: Cohort = clinicians in specialties with >=1 adopter at 5 volunteer sites; clinicians with <5 visits/month excluded (Signal cannot compute measures); adopters vs nonadopters differ in observed mix (Table); D3: Exposure = receiving access (adoption), cleanly dated per clinician; actual use intensity unknown for 452/1809 adopters and some vendors could not provide usage data, so scribe use itself is imperfectly classified (Methods; Table); D4: Co-interventions not measured: site implementation, training and support varied across the 5 sites and are averaged into the estimate (Discussion); non-use among 'adopters' is inherent to the access-based definition; D5: 181273 clinician-month observations; missingness mainly in use-intensity data (handled in sensitivity analyses excluding unknown-intensity adopters, eTable 5); exclusions for low visit volume pre-specified; D6: Outcomes are Epic Signal audit-log measures (EHR-8, DocTime-8, WOW-8) computed identically for adopters and nonadopters; objective, not self-reported; D7: No registration cited; primary outcomes and extensive sensitivity/subgroup analyses pre-described in Methods and reported consistently

D1: Within-clinician matched sessions control clinician-level factors and the model adjusts for patient type (new vs follow-up); BUT participants were experienced, proficient users only (>=30 scribe notes in prior 3 months) - the pre-set self-selection confounder - and clinicians chose which session used the scribe, so session-level case mix could differ (patient-type distribution was similar, P=.72) (Methods; Discussion); D2: Convenience sample: 9 of 27 eligible clinicians selected on scheduling feasibility/observer availability; all were self-selected experienced users, so selection is tied to expected benefit (Methods; Limitations); D3: Intervention cleanly defined per session (Note Buddy vs standard documentation); product and workflow specified; clinician prompt customisation pre-configured and unchanged during the study; D4: Co-interventions: comparator could include unrecorded EHR smart phrases; scribe arm includes manual transfer of notes into the EHR (part of the intervention as deployed); no training/template/staffing changes reported in the window; D5: All 169 observed consultations analysed; no missing time-motion data reported (patient-survey nonresponse, 6/45, affects the survey outcome, not time); D6: Direct observation by 5 trained observers using a standardised worksheet, same observer per clinician across both sessions (reduces inter-observer variance); observers and clinicians unblinded, Hawthorne/observer-expectancy effects acknowledged and eye contact is judgement-based (Limitations); D7: No registration (QI study, SQUIRE reporting); outcomes pre-specified in Methods and all reported in Table 3 including null results

D1: single-arm study with no comparator and no control for baseline documentation load, specialty mix or case complexity (Methods: 'prospective, single-arm feasibility pilot study'); D2: stage 2 encounters sampled at designated sessions when participating physicians were available and stage 1 spanned multiple specialties (Methods, Study Setting); D3: intervention clearly defined as Sahl AI notes generated from recorded audio and evaluated unedited (Methods, Real-World Testing); D4: pipeline was further optimised between stages so version 1 and version 2 are different intervention versions, with at least 30 minutes of training as a co-intervention (Methods); D5: all 64 stage 1 and 55 stage 2 encounters assessed; no missing outcome data reported (Results, Tables 2-3); D6: note-audit addition - sampling: 55 real-world consultations (40 Arabic, 15 English) plus 64 stage 1 assessments; reference standard: evaluators listened to the complete audio recordings; grader blinding: evaluators blinded to patient and physician identities but recruited from the same health cluster, raw audio unredacted so complete blinding could not be assured, and the modified PDQI-9 domains 'have not been formally validated' (Methods; Limitations); D7: no registration or prespecified analysis plan reported; all PDQI-9 domains and totals reported in Table 2

D1: no comparator or adjustment; perceived time saving compared only with respondents' recollection of present practice (Table 4); D2: survey limited to physicians who had used Sahl AI in at least 3 encounters, a self-selected group of engaged users (Methods, Physician Experience); D3: exposure defined by at least 3 encounters of Sahl AI use (Methods); D4: standalone web app without EMR integration and pipeline version changed during the study period (Methods; Limitations); D5: 'the total number of invited physicians was not systematically recorded, a formal response rate cannot be calculated' (Results), so missingness is unquantifiable and likely related to experience; D6: time saving measured only by a single perceived-potential Likert item ('has the potential to save time'), with no timed or audit-log measurement (Table 4); D7: no registration or prespecified plan; survey items fully tabulated in Table 4

D1: no comparator, baseline burnout or adjustment; single post-use perception item only (Table 4); D2: respondents were active users with at least 3 encounters, selected toward engaged users; paper states this 'may introduce selection bias toward more engaged users' (Limitations); D3: exposure defined by at least 3 encounters of use (Methods); D4: training and standalone (non-EMR-integrated) deployment accompanied the intervention (Methods); D5: invited denominator not recorded and response rate cannot be calculated (Results); D6: burnout measured by one agreement item ('can help reduce physician stress/burnout'), not a validated burnout scale, self-reported by users including vendor employees (Table 4; Conflicts of Interest); D7: no registration or prespecified plan reported

D1: no concurrent comparator for note quality; ratings are single-group with no adjustment for provider or session mix (Methods, MHP-Rated Note Quality); D2: feature use was voluntary after a phased rollout and pilot MHPs were a chosen subset asked for feedback, selecting keen users (Methods, Product Development and Deployment); D3: Smart Notes use recorded at note and MHP level with a defined generation workflow and mandatory MHP edit (Methods); D4: phased rollout, live-session release 1 month after launch, training sessions, newsletters and support teams accompanied the intervention (Methods); D5: feedback ratings exist for only 30,519 of 466,139 notes (6.5%), so 93.5% of notes have no quality rating and missingness plausibly depends on satisfaction (Results); D6: note-audit addition - sampling: optional ratings on submitted notes only, no defined audit sample; reference standard: none, ratings are the treating MHP's own thumbs-up/down with no comparison against the encounter record; grader blinding: grader is the note's own clinician and knows the tool, with all authors Talkspace employees (Methods; Conflicts of Interest); D7: no registration or prespecified analysis plan; use, quality and productivity measures all reported

D1: pre-post comparison 1 year apart; authors state confounding by 'natural caseload growth, other changes to the Talkspace platform, or various external factors such as seasonality' cannot be excluded, addressed only partly by a replicated prior-year analysis (Discussion; Multimedia Appendix 1); D2: analysis restricted to MHPs consistently employed across 6 quarters and active in both periods, excluding those who switched employment status - a survivor cohort (Methods, Data Analyses); D3: exposure classified by calendar period rather than individual Smart Notes use, so post-period non-users count as exposed (Methods, MHP Productivity); D4: training programme and platform feature expansion (live sessions) accompanied rollout; other platform changes over the year not controlled (Methods); D5: analysis denominators fall for some outcomes (e.g. contractual clients t1440 vs cohort 1698) with no missing-data handling described (Table 3); D6: hours/sessions/clients from platform logs with stated definitions, but 'administrative and documentation time was not measurable on the platform', so the workload component most relevant to the scribe is unmeasured (Discussion); D7: no registration or prespecified plan; null hours result reported alongside significant session/client increases (Table 3)

D1: no adjustment for baseline documentation load, prior in-person scribe use (8/14) or experience mix; perceived comparisons only (Methods; Results); D2: participants self-selected by opting in, licences allocated by random number generator only among interested eligible EPs, and iPhone ownership was required - early-adopter selection acknowledged in Limitations; D3: access granted on a rolling basis from 1 Sep 2024 with duration of use varying before the survey; exposure not measured per respondent (Methods, Setting and Study Dates); D4: 1-hour mandatory vendor training plus optional sessions accompanied use; in-person scribe availability varied by respondent (Methods); D5: 14 of 16 EPs responded (87.5%) and one item has n=13; no imputation (Results; Methods); D6: efficiency and after-shift time measured only by agreement items on an unvalidated survey ('not adapted from a previously validated scale, and as such, no psychometric testing was performed'), with no timed or audit-log data (Methods); D7: no registration or prespecified plan; descriptive results for all survey items reported with CIs

D4: no documentation training/template/staffing co-interventions stated; learning-curve period (recordings immediately after learning the scribe). D5: hours outcome from surveys: 28/30 baseline, 25/30 follow-up. D6: self-reported hours per week on notes, clinicians aware of scribe use, no log validation in this report. D7: no registration or analysis plan stated; supplement Table A not available.

disagreements: Pass B rated D5 serious; adjudicated moderate - missingness is quantified (28/30, 25/30) with reasons partly described, though outcome-related missingness cannot be excluded; overall serious via D1/D6.
support: D1: as time group - no control, secular/seasonal and adoption effects unhandled; adjustment limited to gender/race/specialty. D2: selected mid-performer volunteers/consenters. D3: exposure period clearly defined. D4: no co-interventions stated; crossover of two products pooled. D5: CBI from 28 baseline / 25 follow-up of 30 consented (one withdrew, missingness described in Table 2 footnote). D6: self-reported Copenhagen Burnout Inventory by unblinded clinicians who knew scribe status; expectation effects likely. D7: no registration/plan; many clinician survey items reported without p values.

disagreements: Pass B rated D5 low; adjudicated moderate because 8/239 patient surveys incomplete and 2 recordings uncoded with item-level missingness in Table 3; overall serious via D1.
support: D1: as above - pre-post without concurrent control; patient groups recruited 1-2 months apart, case-mix differences possible (Table 3 age/employment differ). D2: patients recruited per period (4 per clinician per phase), English-speaking adults only. D3: encounter scribe status clear. D4: no co-interventions stated. D5: 231/239 consented patients completed surveys; 2/232 recordings uncoded (audio/non-English). D6: patient surveys unblinded by design (patients aware of recording/scribe context not stated as blinded); communication coders were blinded - 'Five coders who were unaware of pre or post phase coded written transcripts', double-coding 10%, ICC 0.84-0.99; reference was original audio + transcript. D7: no registration; empathic-opportunity outcomes could not be modelled (68% of recordings had none) and were reported descriptively.

Audit additions for D6 - sampling: all consecutive encounters, 49/53 analysed with exclusions prespecified/described; reference: original encounter audio recording; grader blinding: NOT blinded - 'Raters were not blinded to note type because source-identifying features were intrinsic to the notes', two consultant neurosurgeons scored independently, kappa 0.814, 10 highest-disagreement encounters adjudicated by a third neurosurgeon, panel review finalised errors. D1: paired same-encounter design removes encounter confounding, but verbalisation instruction and audio-as-reference systematically favour AI (authors state net direction uncertain) - moderate. D2: consecutive, no patients declined. D3: AI generation fixed (no diarisation/editing/review, model configuration fixed). D4: clinicians blinded to AI outputs, no co-interventions. D5: 49/53, exclusions explained. D7: no registration; rubric developed a priori by raters, all domains/errors reported.

D1: moderate as quality (verbalisation instruction; timing methods differ by arm). D2: consecutive sample. D3: clear. D4: none. D5: 49/53 analysed. D6: times directly recorded (HW time self-recorded by clinician after each encounter; AI time is system generation time) - measures are objective but not like-for-like. D7: no registration; time reported in Table 1 for all encounters.

disagreements: Pass A rated D1 low (fully paired design); adjudicated moderate - site/language and clinician-grade effects remain and Cologne clinician baseline was markedly lower, so residual confounding by site cannot be excluded; overall moderate either way.
support: Audit additions for D6 - sampling: all 385 paired consultations in frozen dataset (400 planned, 15 excluded for adjudicator non-completion, mainly Cologne); reference: controlled clinical scripts / ground-truth consultation content known in advance; grader blinding: PDQI-9 evaluators blinded to authorship (67 evaluators, 20% inter-rater crossover) but AI notes structurally distinctive so functional unblinding possible (authors state this); PDQI-9 inter-rater reliability low in this cohort (supplement). D1: paired same consultation removes encounter/case-mix confounding; specialty mix not applicable by design; clinician single-hearing vs AI persistent transcript is part of the intervention contrast as prespecified. D2: note-writers openly recruited junior-middle grade, 40 total; allied-health arm excluded before pooling for prespecified reasons. D3: unedited AI first draft vs clinician note clearly defined. D4: simulated, no co-interventions. D5: 385/400 pairs, exclusions follow prespecified complete-pair rule. D7: analysis plan registered on OSF before pooling, departures itemised in supplement, both detection arms reported.

disagreements: Pass B rated D6 low (blinded, externally validated reviewer); adjudicated moderate - detector sensitivity itself differs by note type (human detection 5.2% AI vs 14.0% clinician omissions) and grading reliability was limited, so measurement error may be differential in the human arm.
support: Audit additions for D6 - sampling: all notes in 385 pairs; reference: script ground truth / consultation itself; grader blinding: automated reviewer and severity panel blind to authorship and from different model families than the generator; external validation by 10 independent blinded clinicians on 434 flags (judge-clinician agreement 64% within clinician-clinician range 59%; latent-class sensitivity 0.83, specificity 0.87); human adjudicators flagged errors in free text. D1-D5, D7 as quality group. Severity grading: 3-model panel, agreement on Critical+High cutpoint Gwet AC1 0.57, blind and non-differential.

D1: pre-post with no control group over 5 weeks; none of the prespecified confounders (baseline documentation load, specialty mix, concurrent EHR changes, self-selection) adjusted for; sign test only. D2: '38 volunteer physicians and advanced practice providers' - self-selected volunteers, acknowledged as possibly unrepresentative; benefit absent in lowest-use quartile. D3: Nabla Copilot use clearly defined, notes reviewed/edited and copied into Epic. D4: variable adherence (median 51 encounters, IQR 17-85); no EHR integration; no training/template/staffing co-interventions stated. D5: 35/38 completed both surveys (92%), low missingness. D6: self-reported Stanford PFI by unblinded volunteers; surveys collected in identifiable fashion, which may bias responses. D7: no registration or analysis plan stated; primary PFI outcomes fully reported, qualitative feedback reported selectively in narrative.

Audit additions for D6 - sampling: all eligible encounters from 2 clinics, no sampling undertaken, 400 condition instances; reference: the two generated notes were scored against the modified QNOTE framework, not against encounter audio or a human gold-standard note; grader blinding: primary scoring by GPT-5 LLM pipeline (blinding inherent), human validation on a random 20% sample (n=20 notes) scored independently and blinded to note origin - inter-rater exact agreement 78.4%, human-model exact agreement 73.8%. D1: paired same-encounter design, but the completeness construct mechanically rewards the arm given historical data (vital signs, PMH, comorbidities are inputs to consolidated notes), and condition mix/specialty confounding is limited by stratification (DM/HTN reported separately). D2: complete eligible sample but only 2 clinics and an unstated number of physicians. D3: both documentation methods clearly defined (Navina ambient-only vs RAG consolidated, Claude Sonnet 4). D4: retrospective generation, no deviations/co-interventions applicable. D5: all 400 instances analysed in both arms. D7: no registration; all domains and all 14 items reported including the null q10 result, but authors are vendor employees and scoring pipeline is the vendor's evaluation framework.

Audit additions for D6 - sampling: all 6 scripted scenarios documented by all 7 scribes simultaneously; reference: evaluators were given the case dialogue (scripted encounter) plus rubric and notes; grader blinding: 'Participants were anonymized to all model evaluators' - but evaluators were LLMs only, with no human grading, and one evaluator (OpenAI o1-pro) is the same model family as the system under test (Om built on GPT-o1), a self-preference risk the paper does not address. D1: same scenarios for all scribes control encounter content, but only 6 scenarios and no statistical adjustment/testing. D2: scenarios and scribes selected by authors; commercial scribes anonymised, selection criteria not stated. D3: scribe identities/products clearly separated in generation. D4: simulated, no co-interventions. D5: all notes scored by all 4 evaluators as reported. D7: no registration/plan; results reported mainly as rankings and Om values, with other scribes' scores only in figures - selective numeric reporting.

RoB 2 (week-level randomised design, 26 weeks randomised 2:1, providers told allocation the weekend before). D1: weeks randomly assigned (stated), no sequence/concealment detail and no week-level baseline table - some concerns. D2: providers and patients aware; providers sometimes generated Autoscriber summaries in control weeks (456 vs 387) but paper states they did not appear to use them as basis for notes; patient inclusion left to provider discretion after allocation known - some concerns. D3: workload data from recorded consultations (529) with intervention/control split reported; handling of missing notes not detailed - some concerns. D4: workload is an objective character/operation count from texts, not influenceable by assessor knowledge - low. D5: no trial registration or published analysis plan stated in preprint - some concerns. D6/D7: not applicable (RoB 2 has 5 domains).

RoB 2, errors outcome. D1-D3, D5 as workload group. D4: error counts produced by an LLM counter (GPT-4o) run 10x and averaged, applied identically to both arms against the transcript - sampling: all recorded notes (history/plan sections only); reference: encounter transcript; grader blinding: automated counter, no human grader, but the counter belongs to the same model family used in the Autoscriber pipeline (GPT-4o) and vendor employees are authors, so some concerns rather than low. PDQI-9 was abandoned after a 10-note pilot showed kappa 0.09-1.0 across attributes (reported transparently).

disagreements: Pass B rated D3 high (CARE n unreported, first-half only); adjudicated some concerns - CARE was a secondary outcome with collection window prespecified in Methods (first half), but the unreported denominator is retained as a reporting caveat in support; overall high via D4.
support: RoB 2, patient experience (CARE). D1-D3, D5 as workload group (CARE collected only in the first half of the study, respondent n not reported - D3 some concerns/high in Pass B). D4: CARE is patient self-report; patients knew a recording/scribe study was taking place and consent was obtained before consultations, responses may be influenced by knowledge of the week's allocation - high.

D1: single-arm study; pre values are retrospective recall at one survey, no concurrent control, none of the prespecified confounders (baseline load, specialty mix, concurrent changes, self-selection) can be separated from the scribe effect. D2: critical - survey cohort restricted to fully onboarded sustained users (>=3 months, >100 notes, certificate and conversational-edit use required); discontinuers and non-adopters excluded by design; 39.2% response among invited. D3: exposure (routine Tandem use, v1.0-1.1) defined, but 138,196/376,596 notes (37%) excluded. D4: extensive vendor onboarding/training package (2h + 1h + 1h, management and responsible-use sessions) delivered with the scribe - co-intervention inseparable from tool effect. D5: survey nonresponse handled with IPW sensitivity (results similar), but note-level exclusions and missing transfer status leave outcome-related missingness. D6: primary outcome is recalled self-reported minutes, unblinded, acknowledged to overestimate absolute time ~2-fold in cited literature; objective editing time has no pre comparator and includes idle time. D7: OSF registration Oct 7 2025 was retrospective for metadata (survey prospective), 3 analyses added as exploratory; prespecified outcomes reported.

disagreements: Pass B rated D5 moderate; adjudicated serious - the 37% exclusion of unedited notes plus survey selection/nonresponse leave substantial outcome-related missingness for experience outcomes; overall critical via D2.
support: D1-D5, D7 as time group. D6 (stress/presence): paired Likert recall by unblinded sustained adopters in a single survey; median change 0 for both items despite p<.001, and ease-of-use predictor rests on a ~15-respondent reference group (authors caution); expectation and survivor effects directly target these subjective outcomes - serious.
